sections.text: This checkpoint practices the whole unit. The program is organised in modules, with a module nested inside another (Modules). Some items are private and some are pub, and main brings names in with use (Visibility and use). The checks in main use assert_eq!, the same way the last lesson did (Writing tests). You fill in the missing function bodies.

The starter compiles, but three bodies are marked todo!(), a placeholder that panics with "not yet implemented" when it runs. Look at the shape of the code first. Player lives in mod scoreboard. Its field points is private, and MAX_POINTS is a private constant. The module rank is nested inside scoreboard. A nested module may use the private items of the modules around it, so rank::title can read player.points directly.

At the bottom there is a #[cfg(test)] module with two tests. The app skips it, because it compiles your file without tests. On your own computer, cargo test would run them. The assert_eq! lines in main do the same job here: if a value is wrong, the program panics and shows the left and right values.

add_points: add the amount, then if the total is more than MAX_POINTS, set it to MAX_POINTS. spend: check cost > self.points first and return Err before you change anything. The number of missing points is cost - self.points. title: use a match with range patterns such as 0..=9 and a last arm _ for everything else.

Signatures to match: Player::add_points(&mut self, amount: u32), Player::spend(&mut self, cost: u32) -> Result<(), String>, and rank::title(player: &Player) -> &'static str. The error text is built with format!("{} needs {} more points", name, missing). A failed spend must leave the points unchanged.

exercise.prompt:
Finish the scoreboard. Three bodies are marked todo!().

(1) Player::add_points(&mut self, amount: u32) adds the amount to the points. The points never go above MAX_POINTS (100).

(2) Player::spend(&mut self, cost: u32) -> Result<(), String> subtracts cost from the points and returns Ok(()). If cost is more than the points, it changes nothing and returns Err with the text NAME needs N more points, where NAME is the player's name and N is how many points are missing (for example Ada needs 20 more points).

(3) rank::title(player: &Player) -> &'static str gives rookie for 0 to 9 points, regular for 10 to 49, expert for 50 to 99 and legend for 100.

Keep the pub words as they are, and do not change main. It should print:

Ada: 0 points, rookie
Ada: 40 points, regular
error: Ada needs 20 more points
spent 15
Ada: 100 points, legend
Ada: 49 points, regular
all checks passed

quiz.question: rank::title reads player.points, and points is a private field. Why does this compile?
options: Because private items can be used by the module they are in and by the modules nested inside it
Because rank brings Player in with use

quiz.question: What does use scoreboard::{Player, rank}; at the top of main's file do?
options: It lets main write Player and rank::title instead of the full paths scoreboard::Player and scoreboard::rank::title
It makes Player and rank public
It copies the code of the scoreboard module into main

quiz.question: What does #[cfg(test)] above mod tests do?
options: It marks the module as private
It makes main run the tests every time
The module is compiled only when the tests are built, not in a normal build
